title: Why Joab Was Feared Even by David
paragraphs:
Why Joab Was Feared Even by David
The Most Dangerous Man in Israel Was Not an Enemy of the Throne—He Sat Beside It
There are people who walk into a room and everyone immediately feels safer.
Then there are people who walk into a room and everyone becomes careful.
Joab was the second kind.
He was not a Philistine king. He was not a foreign invader. He was not a giant like Goliath. He was not even a rebel.
He was David’s nephew.
His commander.
His protector.
His enforcer.
And perhaps the most feared man in the kingdom.

The strange thing about Joab is that Scripture never presents him as a simple villain. He was brave when others were afraid. Loyal when others abandoned David. Brilliant in warfare. Relentless against Israel’s enemies.
Yet even David—the giant killer, the warrior king, the man after God’s own heart—often seemed unable to control him.
That reality should make us stop and think.
How dangerous must a man be if even King David feared confronting him?
And what does Joab’s story reveal about the human heart?
Because if we are honest, many of us carry a little Joab inside us.
We love God.
We fight for good causes.
We defend truth.
But somewhere beneath our loyalty lives a part of us that refuses surrender.
A part that still wants control.
A part that believes our way is better than God's way.
And that is where Joab’s tragedy begins.

The first time we see Joab emerge as a major figure, he appears courageous and decisive. Israel needed strong leadership, and Joab provided it. Through countless battles he helped secure David’s kingdom.
Without Joab, David’s throne may never have survived.
Yet Scripture slowly reveals a troubling pattern.
Joab obeyed David when it matched his interests.
He resisted David when it did not.
Outward loyalty concealed inward rebellion.
This is one of the most dangerous spiritual conditions imaginable.
A person can stand close to God's anointed and still remain far from God's heart.
Joab fought for David.
But he never truly submitted to David.
The Hebrew concept behind submission carries the idea of yielding one's will under rightful authority.
Joab never did.
Again and again he chose personal vengeance over divine justice.
Personal ambition over obedience.
Control over trust.
One of the clearest examples occurred after the death of Saul.
A long civil conflict existed between David's supporters and those loyal to Saul's house. During this struggle, Abner, Saul's former military commander, eventually sought peace with David.
David welcomed reconciliation.
The kingdom could finally heal.
The bloodshed could finally end.
But Joab had other plans.
Abner had previously killed Joab’s brother Asahel during battle.
Joab never forgot.
Never forgave.
Never released the offense.
So he secretly murdered Abner despite David's wishes.
Scripture records:
“Then Joab took him aside into the midst of the gate to speak with him privately, and there he struck him in the stomach.” (2 Samuel 3:27)
David was horrified.
His response reveals something remarkable:
“I and my kingdom are forever guiltless before the LORD for the blood of Abner.” (2 Samuel 3:28)
David publicly distanced himself from Joab’s actions because Joab had acted against God's desire for reconciliation.
How many lives are still controlled by old wounds?
How many believers claim to follow Christ while quietly carrying a list of people they refuse to forgive?
Joab teaches us something painful.
Unhealed bitterness eventually demands payment.
And when bitterness becomes a master, even strong people become dangerous.
Years later the pattern repeated.
After Absalom's rebellion, David's son was killed despite David's direct command to spare him.
David had instructed the army:
“Deal gently for my sake with the young man Absalom.” (2 Samuel 18:5)
Yet Joab ignored him.
Again.
Absalom hung helplessly from a tree.
Joab seized the opportunity.
He thrust three spears into Absalom's heart.
The king's command meant nothing compared to Joab's judgment.
The tragedy becomes even deeper when viewed through Scripture's original language.
David's instruction included the Hebrew word לְאַט (le'at), carrying the idea of gentleness, tenderness, and restraint.
David wanted mercy.
Joab wanted results.
David wanted redemption.
Joab wanted elimination.
And in that moment, two kingdoms collided.
The kingdom of grace.
And the kingdom of control.
One sounds remarkably familiar to the Gospel.
The other sounds disturbingly familiar to our flesh.
Joab could win battles.
But he could not surrender his own heart.
That is why David feared him.
Not because Joab was stronger.
Not because Joab had more authority.
But because Joab had become unpredictable.
A man controlled by ambition can become more dangerous than an external enemy.
An enemy attacks from the outside.
Ambition attacks from within.
The Greek New Testament later describes selfish ambition as ἐριθεία (eritheia), a spirit that elevates personal desires above God's will.
It destroys churches.
Destroys families.
Destroys ministries.
Destroys souls.
Joab became a living warning of that reality centuries before the word was written.
Perhaps the most chilling aspect of Joab's story is that he was often right about practical matters.
Many leaders feared Absalom.
Many soldiers likely agreed with Joab's military decisions.
Many probably believed his actions were necessary.
Yet being strategically right does not always mean being spiritually right.
The cross itself proves that.
The religious leaders who condemned Jesus believed they were protecting the nation.
They were politically practical.
But spiritually blind.
Joab repeatedly valued effectiveness above obedience.
And that mistake ultimately destroyed him.
Near the end of David's life another succession crisis emerged.
David declared Solomon would become king.
But Joab backed the wrong candidate.
Adonijah.
Again he opposed God's chosen direction.
Again he trusted his own judgment.
Again he chose control.
When Solomon ascended the throne, Joab fled to the Tabernacle and grabbed the horns of the altar seeking refuge.
But years of rebellion had finally reached their conclusion.
The man who spent his life wielding the sword could not escape its consequences.
His story ended not in victory.
Not in honor.
Not in peace.
But in judgment.
And that is where many people misunderstand the message.
Joab's story is not primarily about military power.
It is about the danger of a heart that remains unsurrendered.
A person can stand near God's work and still resist God's authority.
A person can serve God's kingdom while secretly building their own.
A person can appear faithful while refusing true obedience.
That is why Joab remains one of the most relevant figures in Scripture.
His greatest enemy was never Abner.
Never Absalom.
Never Israel's enemies.
His greatest enemy was the man staring back at him every morning.
The Gospel presents the opposite picture.
Where Joab grasped for control, Jesus surrendered.
Where Joab pursued vengeance, Jesus offered forgiveness.
Where Joab shed blood to preserve power, Jesus shed His blood to save sinners.
The contrast could not be greater.
When Jesus cried from the cross, "Father, forgive them" (Luke 23:34), He revealed a kingdom Joab never understood.
A kingdom where mercy triumphs over judgment.
A kingdom where grace writes a better ending than revenge ever could.
A kingdom where surrendered hearts become truly free.
Perhaps that is why Joab still unsettles readers thousands of years later.
Because his story forces a question.
Am I following Jesus?
Or am I merely serving Him while secretly refusing His authority?
Am I surrendering?
Or am I controlling?
Am I forgiving?
Or am I keeping score?
Am I building Christ's kingdom?
Or my own?
Be honest.
This question reaches deeper than most people expect.
And maybe that is exactly why God preserved Joab's story.
Not merely to teach us about an ancient commander.
But to expose the battle still raging inside every human heart.
Your support helps expand the mission while equipping your own walk with Christ.
Because sometimes the most dangerous enemy is not the one standing against God's kingdom...
It's the part of us that still refuses to kneel before the King.
